facts: $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=x(t)\underset{\sim}{i}+y(t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ says the particle is $x(t)$ across and $y(t)$ up at time $t$.
To find the position at a particular time, substitute that value of $t$ into both components.
The pair $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t)$ are **parametric equations** for the path, with time as the parameter.
The particle's distance from the origin at time $t$ is $\sqrt{x(t)^{2}+y(t)^{2}}$.
The **path** is the curve the particle traces out, and it does not show when the particle reaches each point.
The particle is on the $y$-axis when $x(t)=0$, and on the $x$-axis when $y(t)=0$.
Time is usually restricted to $t\ge0$, so only part of the curve is traced.
steps: Write down the two component functions $x(t)$ and $y(t)$.
Substitute the given value of $t$ into each component.
State the position as a vector or as a point.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-3t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its position when $t=4$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=10\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+10\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its exact position when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
A particle starts at $(-2,4)$. After $t$ seconds it has moved $3t$ units right and $t^{2}$ units down from its starting point. Write its position vector function for $t\ge0$.
A particle moves in a straight line at a steady rate. It is at $(5,8)$ when $t=2$ seconds and at $(17,0)$ when $t=6$ seconds. Find its position vector function.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The coordinate changes occur over $6-2=4$ seconds.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Horizontal change per second}&=\frac{17-5}{4}=3\\\text{Vertical change per second}&=\frac{0-8}{4}=-2\end{aligned}$

Track back two seconds to find the initial position.

$\begin{aligned}x(0)&=5-3(2)=-1\\y(0)&=8-(-2)(2)=12\\\underset{\sim}{r}(t)&=(3t-1)\underset{\sim}{i}+(12-2t)\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2t+1)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t+9)\underset{\sim}{j}$, with coordinates measured in metres. Find its distance from the origin when $t=2$ seconds.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-25)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}-3t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.

(a) Find its position when it crosses the $y$-axis.

(b) Find all times when it is on the $x$-axis.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) On the $y$-axis, $x(t)=0$.

$\begin{aligned}t^{2}-25&=0\\t&=5\end{aligned}$

The negative root is excluded by $t\ge0$.

$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{r}(5)&=(25-25)\underset{\sim}{i}+(25-15)\underset{\sim}{j}\\&=10\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$

(b) On the $x$-axis, $y(t)=0$.

$\begin{aligned}t^{2}-3t&=0\\t(t-3)&=0\end{aligned}$

So $t=0$ or $t=3$.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-t-12)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}-16)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$. Show that it passes through the origin and find when this occurs.
workedExamples.solution_text:
At the origin, both components must be zero at the same time.

$\begin{aligned}t^{2}-t-12&=0\\(t-4)(t+3)&=0\end{aligned}$

For $t\ge0$, the only candidate is $t=4$. Check the other component:

$\begin{aligned}y(4)&=4^{2}-16\\&=0\end{aligned}$

Both components are zero at $t=4$, so the particle passes through the origin then.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(1+t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(4-t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$, where $t$ is measured in seconds. Describe its motion.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t-7)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$, with coordinates measured in metres and $t$ in seconds. Find when it is closest to the origin and its exact distance then.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Minimise the squared distance, which has its minimum at the same time as the distance.

$\begin{aligned}\left|\underset{\sim}{r}(t)\right|^{2}&=(t-7)^{2}+(t+1)^{2}\\&=2t^{2}-12t+50\end{aligned}$

This quadratic opens upwards. Its minimum occurs at

$\begin{aligned}t&=-\frac{-12}{2(2)}\\&=3\text{ s}\end{aligned}$

This time satisfies $t\ge0$.

$\begin{aligned}\left|\underset{\sim}{r}(3)\right|&=\sqrt{(3-7)^{2}+(3+1)^{2}}\\&=\sqrt{32}\\&=4\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$

foundation.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(3t+1)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t-5)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Find its position when $t=4$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-2t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(5-t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Find its position when $t=3$.

A particle starts at the point $(2,-3)$.
After $t$ seconds it has moved $4t$ units to the right and $3t$ units up from its starting point.
Write its position vector function $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t+1)\underset{\sim}{i}+2t\underset{\sim}{j}$.
How far is the particle from the origin when $t=2$?

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t-6)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
At what time is the particle on the $y$-axis?

A particle is at $(-1,7)$ when $t=0$.
Its $x$-coordinate decreases by $2$ each second and its $y$-coordinate never changes.
Write its position vector function $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=4\underset{\sim}{i}+(t-2)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
Describe the motion of the particle.
foundation.solution_text:
$x(t)=4$ for every value of $t$, so the particle stays on the vertical line $x=4$.
$y(t)=t-2$ increases by $1$ each second, starting at $y=-2$.
The particle moves straight up the line $x=4$, starting at $(4,-2)$ and rising $1$ unit each second.

development.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=6\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+6\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Find its exact position when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-9)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
Find the position of the particle when it crosses the $y$-axis.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(3t-1)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t+3)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
How far is the particle from the origin when $t=3$?

At time $t$ a particle's $x$-coordinate is three less than twice $t$, and its $y$-coordinate is the square of $t$.
Write its position vector function $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2+t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(6-t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
Describe the motion of the particle.
development.solution_text:
$x(t)=2+t$ increases by $1$ each second, starting at $x=2$.
$y(t)=6-t$ decreases by $1$ each second, starting at $y=6$.
The particle moves in a straight line from $(2,6)$, going $1$ unit right and $1$ unit down each second.

development.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{3}-4t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}+t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Find its position when $t=2$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2t+3)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}-4t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
Find all times at which the particle is on the $x$-axis.
development.solution_text:
On the $x$-axis the $y$-component is zero.
$t^{2}-4t=0$
$t(t-4)=0$
$t=0$ or $t=4$

mastery.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t-5)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
Find the time at which the particle is closest to the origin, and its exact distance from the origin then.

A particle moves in a straight line at a steady rate.
It is at $(2,5)$ when $t=0$ and at $(14,-3)$ when $t=4$.
Write its position vector function $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$.
mastery.solution_text:
Change in position over $4$ seconds $=(14-2)\underset{\sim}{i}+(-3-5)\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=12\underset{\sim}{i}-8\underset{\sim}{j}$
Change each second $=3\underset{\sim}{i}-2\underset{\sim}{j}$
$\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2+3t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(5-2t)\underset{\sim}{j}$

mastery.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-2t-3)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}-9)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
Show that the particle passes through the origin and find the time at which it does so.
mastery.solution_text:
At the origin both components are zero.
$t^{2}-2t-3=0$
$(t-3)(t+1)=0$
$t=3$ (since $t\ge0$)
$t^{2}-9=0$
$t=3$ (since $t\ge0$)
Both components are zero at $t=3$, so the particle passes through the origin when $t=3$.
